title: Upgrading to TLS Within HTTP/1.1
summary: Explains how to use the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism to start Transport Layer Security (TLS) over an existing TCP connection. This lets a server offer secure and plain HTTP on the same connection endpoint. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2817 defines how HTTP/1.1 can switch an existing TCP connection to TLS instead of requiring a separate connection for secure traffic. When a proxy is involved, CONNECT establishes a tunnel so TLS can protect the connection between the client and the destination server.

questions: how to upgrade http to tls

how does http upgrade to tls
subtitle: How HTTP/1.1 can switch an open connection to TLS and tunnel through proxies.

tldr.problem: Running secure HTTP on a separate port limits the available well-known ports and complicates secure name-based virtual hosting.
tldr.mechanism: A client or server can use HTTP/1.1 Upgrade with the TLS/1.0 token to switch the existing connection. The 426 response signals a required upgrade, while CONNECT creates an end-to-end tunnel through a proxy.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2817 updates RFC 2616 and does not change the https URI scheme. It has been updated by RFC 7230 and RFC 7231.

today: RFC 2817 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2616. It has been updated by RFC 7230 and RFC 7231, and it does not change the https URI scheme.

sections.title: Why Upgrade an Existing Connection
sections.content:
HTTP over SSL was distinguished from plain HTTP by using a different URI scheme and TCP port: http on port 80 and https on port 443. Assigning parallel secure ports to many protocols reduces the number of available well-known ports.

HTTP/1.1 Upgrade can apply TLS to an existing connection. A client can first send a clear HTTP request containing the Host header, allowing the server to select a certificate for a name-based virtual host before the TLS handshake begins.

RFC 2817 does not change how the https URI scheme is interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP can switch an existing connection to TLS rather than requiring a separate port for every secure service. The clear HTTP request can also tell the server which hostname the client wants.

sections.title: Client-Requested Upgrade
sections.content:
A client requests a switch by sending an HTTP/1.1 request with Upgrade: TLS/1.0 and Connection: Upgrade. The Connection header is required when Upgrade appears in an HTTP/1.1 message.

For an optional upgrade, the client may include the offer in a request when an unsecured response would be acceptable. The server may answer normally or accept the switch. If an unsecured response is unacceptable, the client must first send OPTIONS * to request the upgrade.

To accept, the server sends 101 Switching Protocols with the new protocol stack in its Upgrade header. After the TLS handshake succeeds, the server completes the original HTTP request. A failed handshake leads to disconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client offers TLS in an HTTP request, and the server confirms the change with a 101 response. After the handshake succeeds, the server answers the original request over TLS.

sections.title: Server-Requested Upgrade
sections.content:
A server can advertise protocols it is willing to use in the Upgrade response header. To require a change, it can return 426 Upgrade Required and include the required TLS version in Upgrade.

The server should include a human-readable response body explaining why the upgrade is required and any alternatives. A client that accepts TLS must then use the client-requested upgrade procedure; it cannot begin the TLS handshake immediately after receiving 426.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can require TLS by replying with 426 and naming the required protocol. The client must then request the upgrade before starting the TLS handshake.

sections.title: CONNECT Tunnels Through Proxies
sections.content:
Upgrade is hop-by-hop. An Upgrade request sent to a proxy requests a protocol change between the client and that proxy, not between the client and the origin server. TLS needs an end-to-end connection to authenticate the destination and protect against a man-in-the-middle.

The CONNECT method asks a proxy to establish a tunnel to a host and port, such as server.example.com:80. Any 2xx response means the proxy has connected and will pass data through the tunnel. A proxy must not return 2xx unless it has a direct or tunneled connection to the requested authority.

After creating the tunnel, the client can use the HTTP Upgrade operations to start TLS with the destination. A proxy that removes the Upgrade header from a 426 may require the client to establish a tunnel and repeat the request.
sections.plainLanguage: An Upgrade request to a proxy changes only the client-to-proxy connection. CONNECT first creates a tunnel to the destination, so TLS can protect the end-to-end connection.

sections.title: Why 426 Is a Client Error
sections.content:
The RFC assigns 426 as a client-error response rather than a redirect. A client that does not understand a new 3xx status might treat it as a general redirection, look for Location and retry without upgrading.

A 426 response clearly signals that the request cannot be completed without a protocol change. Its Upgrade header identifies which protocol the client needs to use.
sections.plainLanguage: A redirect could make an older client repeat the request without TLS. The 426 response states directly that the requested protocol change is required.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An on-path attacker could remove an Upgrade header, a risk similar to rewriting an https link as http. The RFC says this matters when a server offers the same information over secure and insecure channels. A client that knows TLS is supported can insist on it by sending an Upgrade request with a no-op method such as OPTIONS, and users should examine the server certificate.

CONNECT creates an opaque TCP tunnel, so a proxy cannot inspect the tunneled protocol. The RFC recommends limiting CONNECT authorization to a small number of known ports; this Upgrade mechanism needs onward tunneling only at port 80. Allowing tunnels to other ports could let a client misuse the proxy, for example to relay SMTP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker could remove an upgrade request, so clients should insist on TLS when they know the server supports it. Proxies should restrict CONNECT to a small set of ports because they cannot inspect tunneled traffic.

sections.title: HTTP Status and Upgrade Registries
sections.content:
RFC 2817 asks IANA to maintain registries for HTTP status codes and Upgrade tokens. The status registry includes 426 Upgrade Required. New status codes should receive Standards Track review in the IETF Applications Area.

Upgrade tokens follow the form of a token with an optional product version and are registered First Come First Served. A registration remains registered and must identify a responsible party and contact. This RFC registers TLS/1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps official lists for HTTP response codes and Upgrade tokens. RFC 2817 registers TLS/1.0 as an Upgrade token and 426 as a response code.
